input.system_prompt: Pembuatan cerita dari teks berikut: Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: What factors contributed to the Sri Lankan economic crisis?
input.user_input:
Tentu, ini adalah cerita edukatif tentang krisis ekonomi Sri Lanka yang ditujukan untuk siswa berusia 15-18 tahun.

---

**Judul: Badai di Pulau Permata: Kisah Krisis Ekonomi Sri Lanka**

Dahulu kala, di sebuah pulau yang indah dan subur bernama Sri Lanka, hidup seorang gadis muda bernama Anya. Anya berusia 16 tahun, cerdas, dan selalu ingin tahu. Ia sering mendengar orang dewasa membicarakan "krisis ekonomi" dan "kesulitan hidup" di negaranya. Anya ingin sekali memahami apa yang sebenarnya terjadi.

Suatu sore, Anya bertanya kepada pamannya, Pak Wijaya, seorang pensiunan guru ekonomi. "Paman, mengapa harga-harga menjadi sangat mahal? Mengapa kita sulit mendapatkan bensin dan obat-obatan? Apa yang sebenarnya terjadi pada ekonomi Sri Lanka?"

Pak Wijaya tersenyum lembut. "Pertanyaan bagus, Anya. Krisis ini seperti badai besar yang menghantam sebuah kapal. Banyak faktor yang menyebabkan badai itu datang. Mari paman ceritakan perlahan."

**Faktor Pertama: Kebijakan Pajak yang Terburu-buru (Penguras Lautan)**

"Bayangkan sebuah negara seperti sebuah rumah tangga besar," mulai Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah adalah kepala rumah tangga yang mengumpulkan uang dari pajak warga, seperti gaji. Uang itu digunakan untuk membeli makanan, membayar listrik, membangun jalan, dan lain-lain."

"Pada tahun 2019, pemerintah kita memutuskan untuk memotong banyak pajak. Mereka pikir ini akan mendorong orang untuk berbelanja dan berinvestasi lebih banyak," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Tapi, ibaratnya, mereka terlalu banyak menguras air dari sumur kita. Pendapatan pemerintah langsung anjlok drastis. Akibatnya, uang untuk membiayai kebutuhan negara menjadi sangat kurang."

Anya mengerutkan kening. "Jadi, seperti kalau ayahku gajinya dipotong, kita akan kesulitan membayar kebutuhan rumah tangga?"

"Tepat sekali, Anya! Karena pendapatan negara berkurang, lembaga pemeringkat internasional menurunkan peringkat kredit kita. Ini seperti bank yang menilai seseorang tidak mampu membayar utang, sehingga sulit bagi negara kita untuk meminjam uang lagi dari luar negeri."

**Faktor Kedua: Mencetak Uang Terlalu Banyak (Menggandakan Kertas, Bukan Kekayaan)**

"Karena uang pajak berkurang, pemerintah mencari cara lain untuk membiayai pengeluaran," lanjut Pak Wijaya. "Mereka mulai mencetak uang dalam jumlah besar. Ini seperti kalau kamu kekurangan uang jajan, lalu kamu menggambar uang sendiri di kertas. Apakah uang gambaran itu bisa membeli permen?"

Anya tertawa. "Tentu saja tidak, Paman!"

"Benar. Mencetak uang terlalu banyak tanpa didukung oleh produksi barang dan jasa yang nyata, justru membuat nilai uang kita jatuh. Ini namanya **inflasi**. Barang-barang menjadi sangat mahal karena uang yang beredar terlalu banyak, tapi barangnya tetap sama. Akibatnya, daya beli masyarakat menurun drastis. Ini yang membuat harga bensin, makanan, dan obat-obatan melambung tinggi."

**Faktor Ketiga: Pergeseran Pertanian Organik Mendadak (Menjatuhkan Sekop di Tengah Jalan)**

"Pernahkah kamu mendengar tentang kebijakan pertanian organik?" tanya Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah kita saat itu memutuskan untuk melarang penggunaan pupuk kimia dan pestisida secara tiba-tiba, dengan harapan menjadi negara pertama di dunia yang sepenuhnya organik."

"Kedengarannya bagus, Paman. Lebih sehat, kan?" kata Anya.

"Memang tujuannya baik, Anya. Tapi pelaksanaannya terlalu mendadak dan tanpa persiapan yang matang. Petani kita belum siap dengan metode organik skala besar. Akibatnya, hasil panen, terutama beras dan teh (ekspor utama kita), anjlok drastis. Kita bahkan harus mengimpor beras, padahal dulu kita mandiri pangan."

"Ini seperti kamu sedang membangun rumah, lalu tiba-tiba semua tukang disuruh berhenti memakai alat modern dan hanya boleh memakai alat tradisional. Pekerjaan pasti jadi lambat dan hasilnya kurang maksimal," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Penurunan hasil pertanian ini berdampak besar pada ketersediaan pangan dan juga pemasukan devisa dari ekspor."

**Faktor Keempat: Serangan Teroris dan Pandemi (Badai Tak Terduga)**

"Selain masalah internal, ada juga badai dari luar," kata Pak Wijaya dengan nada prihatin. "Pada tahun 2019, terjadi serangan bom Paskah yang mengerikan. Ini sangat merusak industri pariwisata kita, yang merupakan salah satu sumber utama devisa negara."

"Lalu, pandemi COVID-19 datang. Pembatasan perjalanan dan penutupan perbatasan membuat pariwisata lumpuh total. Pekerja migran kita yang mengirimkan uang dari luar negeri juga banyak yang kehilangan pekerjaan. Akibatnya, pemasukan devisa negara semakin menipis."

Anya menghela napas. "Jadi, devisa itu seperti tabungan negara dalam mata uang asing, Paman?"

"Tepat sekali! Devisa sangat penting untuk membayar impor barang-barang penting seperti bahan bakar, obat-obatan, dan bahan baku industri. Ketika devisa menipis, kita tidak bisa membeli barang-barang ini dari luar negeri, sehingga terjadi kelangkaan dan harga semakin naik."

**Faktor Kelima: Utang Luar Negeri yang Menumpuk (Beban yang Terlalu Berat)**

"Sejak lama, Sri Lanka memiliki kebiasaan meminjam uang dari negara lain dan lembaga internasional," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Dulu, kebanyakan pinjaman untuk proyek pembangunan yang penting. Namun, belakangan ini, banyak pinjaman yang digunakan untuk proyek-proyek 'megah' yang tidak menghasilkan keuntungan ekonomi yang signifikan."

"Utang ini terus menumpuk. Ketika devisa menipis, kita kesulitan membayar cicilan utang. Ini seperti kamu punya banyak utang kartu kredit, tapi gajimu dipotong dan kamu tidak bisa membayar cicilan. Akhirnya, kamu dinyatakan bangkrut."

"Pada tahun 2022, Sri Lanka resmi menyatakan gagal bayar utang. Ini berarti kita tidak mampu membayar utang-utang kita, yang merupakan hal yang sangat serius dan baru pertama kali terjadi sejak kemerdekaan kita."

**Kesimpulan: Pelajaran dari Badai**

"Jadi, Anya," Pak Wijaya mengakhiri penjelasannya, "krisis ekonomi Sri Lanka adalah hasil dari kombinasi beberapa faktor: kebijakan pajak yang salah, pencetakan uang yang berlebihan, perubahan kebijakan pertanian yang terburu-buru, serangan teroris, pandemi, dan beban utang luar negeri yang menumpuk."

"Ini adalah pelajaran berharga bahwa sebuah negara harus memiliki manajemen ekonomi yang hati-hati, perencanaan yang matang, dan tidak boleh mengambil keputusan penting secara terburu-buru tanpa mempertimbangkan dampaknya secara menyeluruh. Kita harus belajar dari kesalahan ini agar badai seperti ini tidak terulang lagi."

Anya mengangguk pelan, wajahnya menunjukkan pemahaman yang lebih dalam. "Terima kasih, Paman. Sekarang aku mengerti mengapa Sri Lanka kita mengalami kesulitan ini. Ini bukan hanya satu masalah, tapi banyak masalah yang terjadi bersamaan."

"Benar, Anya. Dan penting bagi kalian para generasi muda untuk memahami ini, agar kelak kalian bisa menjadi warga negara yang kritis dan berkontribusi dalam membangun masa depan yang lebih baik untuk Sri Lanka."

---
input.criteria:
Consistency (1-5) – ensures the text maintains a uniform style and tone throughout. An educational children's story must have:
1. A consistent narrative voice and tone from beginning to end.
2. Uniform level of formality and writing style across all paragraphs.
3. No unexplained shifts in perspective or storytelling approach.
steps: Check whether the narrative voice and tone remain consistent throughout the story.
Identify any abrupt shifts in style, formality, or perspective that disrupt uniformity.
Verify that the level of educational richness and detail stays uniform from start to finish.
Assign a score for consistency on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 is the lowest and 5 is the highest based on the Evaluation Criteria.

output.reason: The narrative voice and tone remain consistent throughout the story, maintaining an educational yet engaging style suitable for the target audience of 15-18 year olds. There are no abrupt shifts in style or formality. The level of educational richness and detail is uniform from start to finish, with complex economic concepts explained clearly through relatable analogies. The story effectively uses a consistent narrative device (Anya and Pak Wijaya) to deliver information.

Pembuatan cerita dari teks berikut: Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: What factors contributed to the Sri Lankan economic crisis?
contexts:
The Sri Lankan economic crisis is an ongoing crisis in the island country of Sri Lanka that started in 2019. It is the country's worst economic crisis since its independence in 1948. It has led to unprecedented levels of inflation, near-depletion of foreign exchange reserves, shortages of medical supplies, and an increase in prices of basic commodities. The crisis is said to have begun due to multiple compounding factors like tax cuts, money creation, a nationwide policy to shift to organic or biological farming, the 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in Sri Lanka. The subsequent economic hardships resulted in the 2022 Sri Lankan protests.
Sri Lanka had been earmarked for sovereign default, as the remaining foreign exchange reserves of US$1.9 billion as of March 2022 would not be sufficient to pay the country's foreign debt obligations for 2022, with $4 billion to be repaid. An International Sovereign Bond repayment of $1 billion was due to be paid by the government in July 2022. Bloomberg reported that Sri Lanka had a total of $8.6 billion in repayments due in 2022, including both local debt and foreign debt. In April 2022, the Sri Lankan government announced that it was defaulting, making it the first sovereign default in Sri Lankan history since its independence in 1948 and the first state in the Asia-Pacific region to enter sovereign default in the 21st century.In June 2022, then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said in parliament that the economy had collapsed, leaving it unable to pay for essentials.In September 2022, a United Nations report said that the economic crisis is a result of officials' impunity for human rights abuses and economic crimes. According to the Sri Lankan finance ministry, the country's foreign reserves had grown by 23.5% from US$1.7 billion in September 2022 to US$2.1 billion in February 2023, representing a US$400 million increase. Sri Lanka teeters on the edge of financial insolvency and has halted repayments on its international debts.

Background
According to W. A. Wijewardena, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the country was a long way into an economic crisis in 2015. The government that came into power in 2015 knew this and had been warned by the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka about a number of risks. While the then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe in 2015 had presented a strong economic policy to address the situation, the coalition government could not get the policy pushed through Parliament, which would eventually result in further policy confusion in the coming months.The government did not adequately address the economic warnings and emerging dangers, consuming itself in other government related activities such as "constitutional reforms". Certain practices, including those used by the Ministry of Finance led by Ravi Karunanayake, were globally frowned upon. Election related economic decisions were pushed such as excessive distribution of freebies. The Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka's 2014 State of the Economy Report highlighted hot money, worrying borrowing practices, temporary and superficial quick-fixes and monopoly of foreign direct investment flow into the hospitality sector.Further political turmoil in 2018 worsened the economic outlook. By that time the government had carried out several reforms under an IMF supported program towards fiscal monetary consolidation and had successfully controlled inflation. These reforms included an automatic fuel pricing formula which significantly reduced fiscal risks posed by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), raised the value-added tax (VAT) rate from 11 percent to 15 percent, and broadened the VAT base by removing exemptions. Many of the reforms were reversed by the new government after the 2019 elections.Under Maithripala Sirisena administration, the 2019 Central Bank Bill was drafted to make the Central Bank independent from political influence by banning the Treasury Secretary and any member of the Government from becoming members of the Monetary Board. Money printing was also to be banned under this bill, as it states: "The Central Bank shall not purchase securities issued by the government, by any government-owned entity, or any other public entity in the primary market." Then Central Bank Governor, Indrajit Coomaraswamy, noted Balance of Payments issues, increased inflation, and asset bubbles as reasons for the ban. The Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna Party opposed an independent Central Bank and discarded the bill as soon as they came to power.Many experts compared Lebanon's economic situation with that of Sri Lanka and had warned that Sri Lanka too was on the way to defaulting on its sovereign bonds. Both nations had similar issues, including deep economic crises occurring after their successive governments piled up unsustainable debts following the end of civil wars. To reduce the inflation and control the economy crisis in April 2022, Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe was appointed as the 17th Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) to replace Ajith Nivard Cabraal.

Causes
Tax cuts and money creation
The Government of Sri Lanka under president Gotabaya Rajapaksa made large tax cuts that affected government revenue and fiscal policies, causing budget deficits to soar.  These cuts included increased tax-free thresholds that resulted in a 33.5% decline in registered taxpayers, reducing VAT to 8%, reducing corporate tax from  28% to 24%, the abolishment of the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax and the 2% “nation-building tax” which financed infrastructure development. The massive loss of tax revenue resulted in rating agencies downgrading the sovereign credit rating making it harder to take more debt. In 2021 P. B. Jayasundera stated that President Rajapaksa was aware of the loss of revenue but considered it an "investment" and had no plans of increasing taxes for another 5 years.To cover government spending, the Central Bank began printing money in record amounts ignoring advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stop printing money and instead hike interest rates and raise taxes while cutting spending.  The IMF warned that continuing to print money would lead to an economic implosion. The tax cuts were also opposed by the former Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera who noted that as the Sri Lankan government already had far less tax revenue relative to most countries which combined with its high debt load tax cuts would be dangerous. Samaraweera predicted that “If these proposals are implemented like this not only will the entire country go bankrupt, but the entire country will become another Venezuela or another Greece.”On 6 April 2022, the CBSL allegedly printed 119.08 billion rupees, making it the highest reported amount printed on a single day by the CBSL for the year 2022. The total money added to financial markets for the year 2022 increased to Rs. 432.76 billion.

External debt
Until mid-2000s, the Sri Lankan debt was mainly from multilateral lending agencies, after which it was reoriented under the leadership of Mahinda Rajapaksa to foreign investors and lenders. Sri Lanka issues its first international sovereign bond in 2007, with high interest rates to incentivise investors. According to commentators, the money was used to fund vanity projects rather than projects of national utility.Sri Lanka's foreign debt increased substantially, going from US$11.3 billion in 2005 to $56.3 billion in 2020. While foreign debt was about 42% of the GDP in 2019, it rose to 119% of its GDP in 2021. By February 2022, the country had only $2.31 billion left in its reserves, yet faces debt repayments of around $4 billion in 2022, which also includes a $1 billion international sovereign bond (ISB) maturing in July.In 2020, US economist Joseph Eugene Stiglitz, published a report that blamed the quantitative easing policy made by US banks after 2008, for exporting debt bubbles to deve

. This has raised concerns about the country's ability to meet its financial obligations and maintain its economic stability.

The declining reserves can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, the COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted the country's economy, leading to a decrease in export revenues and foreign direct investment. This has resulted in a decline in foreign currency inflows, putting pressure on the country's reserves.

Secondly, the country has been facing a persistent current account deficit, meaning that it is importing more goods and services than it is exporting. This has further strained the country's reserves as it needs to use foreign currency to pay for these imports.

Additionally, the country has been grappling with high levels of external debt. The debt repayments, including the maturing ISB, add to the financial burden and put further strain on the country's reserves.

To address these challenges, the country may need to take several measures. Firstly, it could seek financial assistance from international organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or the World Bank. This could provide the country with the necessary funds to meet its debt obligations and stabilize its reserves.

Secondly, the country could implement policies to boost its export revenues and reduce its reliance on imports. This could include promoting domestic industries, diversifying its export markets, and improving the business environment to attract foreign investment.

input.question: What factors contributed to the Sri Lankan economic crisis?
input.user_message: Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: What factors contributed to the Sri Lankan economic crisis?
merged_contexts:
The Sri Lankan economic crisis is an ongoing crisis in the island country of Sri Lanka that started in 2019. It is the country's worst economic crisis since its independence in 1948. It has led to unprecedented levels of inflation, near-depletion of foreign exchange reserves, shortages of medical supplies, and an increase in prices of basic commodities. The crisis is said to have begun due to multiple compounding factors like tax cuts, money creation, a nationwide policy to shift to organic or biological farming, the 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in Sri Lanka. The subsequent economic hardships resulted in the 2022 Sri Lankan protests.
Sri Lanka had been earmarked for sovereign default, as the remaining foreign exchange reserves of US$1.9 billion as of March 2022 would not be sufficient to pay the country's foreign debt obligations for 2022, with $4 billion to be repaid. An International Sovereign Bond repayment of $1 billion was due to be paid by the government in July 2022. Bloomberg reported that Sri Lanka had a total of $8.6 billion in repayments due in 2022, including both local debt and foreign debt. In April 2022, the Sri Lankan government announced that it was defaulting, making it the first sovereign default in Sri Lankan history since its independence in 1948 and the first state in the Asia-Pacific region to enter sovereign default in the 21st century.In June 2022, then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said in parliament that the economy had collapsed, leaving it unable to pay for essentials.In September 2022, a United Nations report said that the economic crisis is a result of officials' impunity for human rights abuses and economic crimes. According to the Sri Lankan finance ministry, the country's foreign reserves had grown by 23.5% from US$1.7 billion in September 2022 to US$2.1 billion in February 2023, representing a US$400 million increase. Sri Lanka teeters on the edge of financial insolvency and has halted repayments on its international debts.

Background
According to W. A. Wijewardena, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the country was a long way into an economic crisis in 2015. The government that came into power in 2015 knew this and had been warned by the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka about a number of risks. While the then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe in 2015 had presented a strong economic policy to address the situation, the coalition government could not get the policy pushed through Parliament, which would eventually result in further policy confusion in the coming months.The government did not adequately address the economic warnings and emerging dangers, consuming itself in other government related activities such as "constitutional reforms". Certain practices, including those used by the Ministry of Finance led by Ravi Karunanayake, were globally frowned upon. Election related economic decisions were pushed such as excessive distribution of freebies. The Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka's 2014 State of the Economy Report highlighted hot money, worrying borrowing practices, temporary and superficial quick-fixes and monopoly of foreign direct investment flow into the hospitality sector.Further political turmoil in 2018 worsened the economic outlook. By that time the government had carried out several reforms under an IMF supported program towards fiscal monetary consolidation and had successfully controlled inflation. These reforms included an automatic fuel pricing formula which significantly reduced fiscal risks posed by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), raised the value-added tax (VAT) rate from 11 percent to 15 percent, and broadened the VAT base by removing exemptions. Many of the reforms were reversed by the new government after the 2019 elections.Under Maithripala Sirisena administration, the 2019 Central Bank Bill was drafted to make the Central Bank independent from political influence by banning the Treasury Secretary and any member of the Government from becoming members of the Monetary Board. Money printing was also to be banned under this bill, as it states: "The Central Bank shall not purchase securities issued by the government, by any government-owned entity, or any other public entity in the primary market." Then Central Bank Governor, Indrajit Coomaraswamy, noted Balance of Payments issues, increased inflation, and asset bubbles as reasons for the ban. The Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna Party opposed an independent Central Bank and discarded the bill as soon as they came to power.Many experts compared Lebanon's economic situation with that of Sri Lanka and had warned that Sri Lanka too was on the way to defaulting on its sovereign bonds. Both nations had similar issues, including deep economic crises occurring after their successive governments piled up unsustainable debts following the end of civil wars. To reduce the inflation and control the economy crisis in April 2022, Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe was appointed as the 17th Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) to replace Ajith Nivard Cabraal.

Causes
Tax cuts and money creation
The Government of Sri Lanka under president Gotabaya Rajapaksa made large tax cuts that affected government revenue and fiscal policies, causing budget deficits to soar.  These cuts included increased tax-free thresholds that resulted in a 33.5% decline in registered taxpayers, reducing VAT to 8%, reducing corporate tax from  28% to 24%, the abolishment of the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax and the 2% “nation-building tax” which financed infrastructure development. The massive loss of tax revenue resulted in rating agencies downgrading the sovereign credit rating making it harder to take more debt. In 2021 P. B. Jayasundera stated that President Rajapaksa was aware of the loss of revenue but considered it an "investment" and had no plans of increasing taxes for another 5 years.To cover government spending, the Central Bank began printing money in record amounts ignoring advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stop printing money and instead hike interest rates and raise taxes while cutting spending.  The IMF warned that continuing to print money would lead to an economic implosion. The tax cuts were also opposed by the former Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera who noted that as the Sri Lankan government already had far less tax revenue relative to most countries which combined with its high debt load tax cuts would be dangerous. Samaraweera predicted that “If these proposals are implemented like this not only will the entire country go bankrupt, but the entire country will become another Venezuela or another Greece.”On 6 April 2022, the CBSL allegedly printed 119.08 billion rupees, making it the highest reported amount printed on a single day by the CBSL for the year 2022. The total money added to financial markets for the year 2022 increased to Rs. 432.76 billion.

External debt
Until mid-2000s, the Sri Lankan debt was mainly from multilateral lending agencies, after which it was reoriented under the leadership of Mahinda Rajapaksa to foreign investors and lenders. Sri Lanka issues its first international sovereign bond in 2007, with high interest rates to incentivise investors. According to commentators, the money was used to fund vanity projects rather than projects of national utility.Sri Lanka's foreign debt increased substantially, going from US$11.3 billion in 2005 to $56.3 billion in 2020. While foreign debt was about 42% of the GDP in 2019, it rose to 119% of its GDP in 2021. By February 2022, the country had only $2.31 billion left in its reserves, yet faces debt repayments of around $4 billion in 2022, which also includes a $1 billion international sovereign bond (ISB) maturing in July.In 2020, US economist Joseph Eugene Stiglitz, published a report that blamed the quantitative easing policy made by US banks after 2008, for exporting debt bubbles to deve

. This has raised concerns about the country's ability to meet its financial obligations and maintain its economic stability.

This has resulted in a decline in foreign currency inflows, putting pressure on the country's reserves.

Secondly, the country has been facing a persistent current account deficit, meaning that it is importing more goods and services than it is exporting. This has further strained the country's reserves as it needs to use foreign currency to pay for these imports.

Additionally, the country has been grappling with high levels of external debt. The debt repayments, including the maturing ISB, add to the financial burden and put further strain on the country's reserves.

To address these challenges, the country may need to take several measures. Firstly, it could seek financial assistance from international organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or the World Bank. This could provide the country with the necessary funds to meet its debt obligations and stabilize its reserves.

Secondly, the country could implement policies to boost its export revenues and reduce its reliance on imports. This could include promoting domestic industries, diversifying its export markets, and improving the business environment to attract foreign investment.

Furthermore, the country could explore options to restructure its debt, such as negotiating with creditors to extend repayment periods or reduce interest rates. This could help alleviate the immediate financial pressure and provide the country with more breathing room to manage its reserves.

Overall, the declining reserves and upcoming debt repayments pose significant challenges for the country's economic stability. However, with the right measures and support from international organizations, the country can work towards addressing these challenges and ensuring its long-term financial sustainability.

output.final_story:
Tentu, ini adalah cerita edukatif tentang krisis ekonomi Sri Lanka yang ditujukan untuk siswa berusia 15-18 tahun.

---

**Judul: Badai di Pulau Permata: Kisah Krisis Ekonomi Sri Lanka**

Dahulu kala, di sebuah pulau yang indah dan subur bernama Sri Lanka, hidup seorang gadis muda bernama Anya. Anya berusia 16 tahun, cerdas, dan selalu ingin tahu. Ia sering mendengar orang dewasa membicarakan "krisis ekonomi" dan "kesulitan hidup" di negaranya. Anya ingin sekali memahami apa yang sebenarnya terjadi.

Suatu sore, Anya bertanya kepada pamannya, Pak Wijaya, seorang pensiunan guru ekonomi. "Paman, mengapa harga-harga menjadi sangat mahal? Mengapa kita sulit mendapatkan bensin dan obat-obatan? Apa yang sebenarnya terjadi pada ekonomi Sri Lanka?"

Pak Wijaya tersenyum lembut. "Pertanyaan bagus, Anya. Krisis ini seperti badai besar yang menghantam sebuah kapal. Banyak faktor yang menyebabkan badai itu datang. Mari paman ceritakan perlahan."

**Faktor Pertama: Kebijakan Pajak yang Terburu-buru (Penguras Lautan)**

"Bayangkan sebuah negara seperti sebuah rumah tangga besar," mulai Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah adalah kepala rumah tangga yang mengumpulkan uang dari pajak warga, seperti gaji. Uang itu digunakan untuk membeli makanan, membayar listrik, membangun jalan, dan lain-lain."

"Pada tahun 2019, pemerintah kita memutuskan untuk memotong banyak pajak. Mereka pikir ini akan mendorong orang untuk berbelanja dan berinvestasi lebih banyak," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Tapi, ibaratnya, mereka terlalu banyak menguras air dari sumur kita. Pendapatan pemerintah langsung anjlok drastis. Akibatnya, uang untuk membiayai kebutuhan negara menjadi sangat kurang."

Anya mengerutkan kening. "Jadi, seperti kalau ayahku gajinya dipotong, kita akan kesulitan membayar kebutuhan rumah tangga?"

"Tepat sekali, Anya! Karena pendapatan negara berkurang, lembaga pemeringkat internasional menurunkan peringkat kredit kita. Ini seperti bank yang menilai seseorang tidak mampu membayar utang, sehingga sulit bagi negara kita untuk meminjam uang lagi dari luar negeri."

**Faktor Kedua: Mencetak Uang Terlalu Banyak (Menggandakan Kertas, Bukan Kekayaan)**

"Karena uang pajak berkurang, pemerintah mencari cara lain untuk membiayai pengeluaran," lanjut Pak Wijaya. "Mereka mulai mencetak uang dalam jumlah besar. Ini seperti kalau kamu kekurangan uang jajan, lalu kamu menggambar uang sendiri di kertas. Apakah uang gambaran itu bisa membeli permen?"

Anya tertawa. "Tentu saja tidak, Paman!"

"Benar. Mencetak uang terlalu banyak tanpa didukung oleh produksi barang dan jasa yang nyata, justru membuat nilai uang kita jatuh. Ini namanya **inflasi**. Barang-barang menjadi sangat mahal karena uang yang beredar terlalu banyak, tapi barangnya tetap sama. Akibatnya, daya beli masyarakat menurun drastis. Ini yang membuat harga bensin, makanan, dan obat-obatan melambung tinggi."

**Faktor Ketiga: Pergeseran Pertanian Organik Mendadak (Menjatuhkan Sekop di Tengah Jalan)**

"Pernahkah kamu mendengar tentang kebijakan pertanian organik?" tanya Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah kita saat itu memutuskan untuk melarang penggunaan pupuk kimia dan pestisida secara tiba-tiba, dengan harapan menjadi negara pertama di dunia yang sepenuhnya organik."

"Kedengarannya bagus, Paman. Lebih sehat, kan?" kata Anya.

"Memang tujuannya baik, Anya. Tapi pelaksanaannya terlalu mendadak dan tanpa persiapan yang matang. Petani kita belum siap dengan metode organik skala besar. Akibatnya, hasil panen, terutama beras dan teh (ekspor utama kita), anjlok drastis. Kita bahkan harus mengimpor beras, padahal dulu kita mandiri pangan."

"Ini seperti kamu sedang membangun rumah, lalu tiba-tiba semua tukang disuruh berhenti memakai alat modern dan hanya boleh memakai alat tradisional. Pekerjaan pasti jadi lambat dan hasilnya kurang maksimal," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Penurunan hasil pertanian ini berdampak besar pada ketersediaan pangan dan juga pemasukan devisa dari ekspor."

**Faktor Keempat: Serangan Teroris dan Pandemi (Badai Tak Terduga)**

"Selain masalah internal, ada juga badai dari luar," kata Pak Wijaya dengan nada prihatin. "Pada tahun 2019, terjadi serangan bom Paskah yang mengerikan. Ini sangat merusak industri pariwisata kita, yang merupakan salah satu sumber utama devisa negara."

"Lalu, pandemi COVID-19 datang. Pembatasan perjalanan dan penutupan perbatasan membuat pariwisata lumpuh total. Pekerja migran kita yang mengirimkan uang dari luar negeri juga banyak yang kehilangan pekerjaan. Akibatnya, pemasukan devisa negara semakin menipis."

Anya menghela napas. "Jadi, devisa itu seperti tabungan negara dalam mata uang asing, Paman?"

"Tepat sekali! Devisa sangat penting untuk membayar impor barang-barang penting seperti bahan bakar, obat-obatan, dan bahan baku industri. Ketika devisa menipis, kita tidak bisa membeli barang-barang ini dari luar negeri, sehingga terjadi kelangkaan dan harga semakin naik."

**Faktor Kelima: Utang Luar Negeri yang Menumpuk (Beban yang Terlalu Berat)**

"Sejak lama, Sri Lanka memiliki kebiasaan meminjam uang dari negara lain dan lembaga internasional," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Dulu, kebanyakan pinjaman untuk proyek pembangunan yang penting. Namun, belakangan ini, banyak pinjaman yang digunakan untuk proyek-proyek 'megah' yang tidak menghasilkan keuntungan ekonomi yang signifikan."

"Utang ini terus menumpuk. Ketika devisa menipis, kita kesulitan membayar cicilan utang. Ini seperti kamu punya banyak utang kartu kredit, tapi gajimu dipotong dan kamu tidak bisa membayar cicilan. Akhirnya, kamu dinyatakan bangkrut."

"Pada tahun 2022, Sri Lanka resmi menyatakan gagal bayar utang. Ini berarti kita tidak mampu membayar utang-utang kita, yang merupakan hal yang sangat serius dan baru pertama kali terjadi sejak kemerdekaan kita."

**Kesimpulan: Pelajaran dari Badai**

"Jadi, Anya," Pak Wijaya mengakhiri penjelasannya, "krisis ekonomi Sri Lanka adalah hasil dari kombinasi beberapa faktor: kebijakan pajak yang salah, pencetakan uang yang berlebihan, perubahan kebijakan pertanian yang terburu-buru, serangan teroris, pandemi, dan beban utang luar negeri yang menumpuk."

"Ini adalah pelajaran berharga bahwa sebuah negara harus memiliki manajemen ekonomi yang hati-hati, perencanaan yang matang, dan tidak boleh mengambil keputusan penting secara terburu-buru tanpa mempertimbangkan dampaknya secara menyeluruh. Kita harus belajar dari kesalahan ini agar badai seperti ini tidak terulang lagi."

Anya mengangguk pelan, wajahnya menunjukkan pemahaman yang lebih dalam. "Terima kasih, Paman. Sekarang aku mengerti mengapa Sri Lanka kita mengalami kesulitan ini. Ini bukan hanya satu masalah, tapi banyak masalah yang terjadi bersamaan."

"Benar, Anya. Dan penting bagi kalian para generasi muda untuk memahami ini, agar kelak kalian bisa menjadi warga negara yang kritis dan berkontribusi dalam membangun masa depan yang lebih baik untuk Sri Lanka."

**Judul: Badai di Pulau Permata: Kisah Krisis Ekonomi Sri Lanka**

Dahulu kala, di sebuah pulau yang indah dan subur bernama Sri Lanka, hidup seorang gadis muda bernama Anya. Anya berusia 16 tahun, cerdas, dan selalu ingin tahu. Pak Wijaya tersenyum lembut. "Pertanyaan bagus, Anya. Krisis ini seperti badai besar yang menghantam sebuah kapal. Banyak faktor yang menyebabkan badai itu datang. Mari paman ceritakan perlahan."

"Bayangkan sebuah negara seperti sebuah rumah tangga besar," mulai Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah adalah kepala rumah tangga yang mengumpulkan uang dari pajak warga, seperti gaji. Uang itu digunakan untuk membeli makanan, membayar listrik, membangun jalan, dan lain-lain."

"Pada tahun 2019, pemerintah kita memutuskan untuk memotong banyak pajak. Mereka pikir ini akan mendorong orang untuk berbelanja dan berinvestasi lebih banyak," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Tapi, ibaratnya, mereka terlalu banyak menguras air dari sumur kita. Pendapatan pemerintah langsung anjlok drastis. Akibatnya, uang untuk membiayai kebutuhan negara menjadi sangat kurang."

Anya mengerutkan kening. "Jadi, seperti kalau ayahku gajinya dipotong, kita akan kesulitan membayar kebutuhan rumah tangga?"

"Tepat sekali, Anya! Karena pendapatan negara berkurang, lembaga pemeringkat internasional menurunkan peringkat kredit kita. Ini seperti bank yang menilai seseorang tidak mampu membayar utang, sehingga sulit bagi negara kita untuk meminjam uang lagi dari luar negeri."

**Faktor Kedua: Mencetak Uang Terlalu Banyak (Menggandakan Kertas, Bukan Kekayaan)**

"Karena uang pajak berkurang, pemerintah mencari cara lain untuk membiayai pengeluaran," lanjut Pak Wijaya. "Mereka mulai mencetak uang dalam jumlah besar. Ini seperti kalau kamu kekurangan uang jajan, lalu kamu menggambar uang sendiri di kertas. Apakah uang gambaran itu bisa membeli permen?"

Anya tertawa. "Tentu saja tidak, Paman!"

Barang-barang menjadi sangat mahal karena uang yang beredar terlalu banyak, tapi barangnya tetap sama. Akibatnya, daya beli masyarakat menurun drastis. Ini yang membuat harga bensin, makanan, dan obat-obatan melambung tinggi."

**Faktor Ketiga: Pergeseran Pertanian Organik Mendadak (Menjatuhkan Sekop di Tengah Jalan)**

"Pernahkah kamu mendengar tentang kebijakan pertanian organik?" tanya Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah kita saat itu memutuskan untuk melarang penggunaan pupuk kimia dan pestisida secara tiba-tiba, dengan harapan menjadi negara pertama di dunia yang sepenuhnya organik."

"Memang tujuannya baik, Anya. Tapi pelaksanaannya terlalu mendadak dan tanpa persiapan yang matang. Petani kita belum siap dengan metode organik skala besar. Pekerjaan pasti jadi lambat dan hasilnya kurang maksimal," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Penurunan hasil pertanian ini berdampak besar pada ketersediaan pangan dan juga pemasukan devisa dari ekspor."

"Selain masalah internal, ada juga badai dari luar," kata Pak Wijaya dengan nada prihatin. "Pada tahun 2019, terjadi serangan bom Paskah yang mengerikan. Ini sangat merusak industri pariwisata kita, yang merupakan salah satu sumber utama devisa negara."

"Sejak lama, Sri Lanka memiliki kebiasaan meminjam uang dari negara lain dan lembaga internasional," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Dulu, kebanyakan pinjaman untuk proyek pembangunan yang penting. "Pada tahun 2022, Sri Lanka resmi menyatakan gagal bayar utang. Ini berarti kita tidak mampu membayar utang-utang kita, yang merupakan hal yang sangat serius dan baru pertama kali terjadi sejak kemerdekaan kita."

"Ini adalah pelajaran berharga bahwa sebuah negara harus memiliki manajemen ekonomi yang hati-hati, perencanaan yang matang, dan tidak boleh mengambil keputusan penting secara terburu-buru tanpa mempertimbangkan dampaknya secara menyeluruh. Kita harus belajar dari kesalahan ini agar badai seperti ini tidak terulang lagi."

Anya mengangguk pelan, wajahnya menunjukkan pemahaman yang lebih dalam. "Terima kasih, Paman. Sekarang aku mengerti mengapa Sri Lanka kita mengalami kesulitan ini. Ini bukan hanya satu masalah, tapi banyak masalah yang terjadi bersamaan."

"Benar, Anya. Dan penting bagi kalian para generasi muda untuk memahami ini, agar kelak kalian bisa menjadi warga negara yang kritis dan berkontribusi dalam membangun masa depan yang lebih baik untuk Sri Lanka."

contexts:
The Sri Lankan economic crisis is an ongoing crisis in the island country of Sri Lanka that started in 2019. It is the country's worst economic crisis since its independence in 1948. It has led to unprecedented levels of inflation, near-depletion of foreign exchange reserves, shortages of medical supplies, and an increase in prices of basic commodities. The crisis is said to have begun due to multiple compounding factors like tax cuts, money creation, a nationwide policy to shift to organic or biological farming, the 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in Sri Lanka. The subsequent economic hardships resulted in the 2022 Sri Lankan protests.
Sri Lanka had been earmarked for sovereign default, as the remaining foreign exchange reserves of US$1.9 billion as of March 2022 would not be sufficient to pay the country's foreign debt obligations for 2022, with $4 billion to be repaid. An International Sovereign Bond repayment of $1 billion was due to be paid by the government in July 2022. Bloomberg reported that Sri Lanka had a total of $8.6 billion in repayments due in 2022, including both local debt and foreign debt. In April 2022, the Sri Lankan government announced that it was defaulting, making it the first sovereign default in Sri Lankan history since its independence in 1948 and the first state in the Asia-Pacific region to enter sovereign default in the 21st century.In June 2022, then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said in parliament that the economy had collapsed, leaving it unable to pay for essentials.In September 2022, a United Nations report said that the economic crisis is a result of officials' impunity for human rights abuses and economic crimes. According to the Sri Lankan finance ministry, the country's foreign reserves had grown by 23.5% from US$1.7 billion in September 2022 to US$2.1 billion in February 2023, representing a US$400 million increase. Sri Lanka teeters on the edge of financial insolvency and has halted repayments on its international debts.

Background
According to W. A. Wijewardena, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the country was a long way into an economic crisis in 2015. The government that came into power in 2015 knew this and had been warned by the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka about a number of risks. While the then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe in 2015 had presented a strong economic policy to address the situation, the coalition government could not get the policy pushed through Parliament, which would eventually result in further policy confusion in the coming months.The government did not adequately address the economic warnings and emerging dangers, consuming itself in other government related activities such as "constitutional reforms". Certain practices, including those used by the Ministry of Finance led by Ravi Karunanayake, were globally frowned upon. Election related economic decisions were pushed such as excessive distribution of freebies. The Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka's 2014 State of the Economy Report highlighted hot money, worrying borrowing practices, temporary and superficial quick-fixes and monopoly of foreign direct investment flow into the hospitality sector.Further political turmoil in 2018 worsened the economic outlook. By that time the government had carried out several reforms under an IMF supported program towards fiscal monetary consolidation and had successfully controlled inflation. These reforms included an automatic fuel pricing formula which significantly reduced fiscal risks posed by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), raised the value-added tax (VAT) rate from 11 percent to 15 percent, and broadened the VAT base by removing exemptions. Many of the reforms were reversed by the new government after the 2019 elections.Under Maithripala Sirisena administration, the 2019 Central Bank Bill was drafted to make the Central Bank independent from political influence by banning the Treasury Secretary and any member of the Government from becoming members of the Monetary Board. Money printing was also to be banned under this bill, as it states: "The Central Bank shall not purchase securities issued by the government, by any government-owned entity, or any other public entity in the primary market." Then Central Bank Governor, Indrajit Coomaraswamy, noted Balance of Payments issues, increased inflation, and asset bubbles as reasons for the ban. The Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna Party opposed an independent Central Bank and discarded the bill as soon as they came to power.Many experts compared Lebanon's economic situation with that of Sri Lanka and had warned that Sri Lanka too was on the way to defaulting on its sovereign bonds. Both nations had similar issues, including deep economic crises occurring after their successive governments piled up unsustainable debts following the end of civil wars. To reduce the inflation and control the economy crisis in April 2022, Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe was appointed as the 17th Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) to replace Ajith Nivard Cabraal.

Causes
Tax cuts and money creation
The Government of Sri Lanka under president Gotabaya Rajapaksa made large tax cuts that affected government revenue and fiscal policies, causing budget deficits to soar.  These cuts included increased tax-free thresholds that resulted in a 33.5% decline in registered taxpayers, reducing VAT to 8%, reducing corporate tax from  28% to 24%, the abolishment of the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax and the 2% “nation-building tax” which financed infrastructure development. The massive loss of tax revenue resulted in rating agencies downgrading the sovereign credit rating making it harder to take more debt. In 2021 P. B. Jayasundera stated that President Rajapaksa was aware of the loss of revenue but considered it an "investment" and had no plans of increasing taxes for another 5 years.To cover government spending, the Central Bank began printing money in record amounts ignoring advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stop printing money and instead hike interest rates and raise taxes while cutting spending.  The IMF warned that continuing to print money would lead to an economic implosion. The tax cuts were also opposed by the former Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera who noted that as the Sri Lankan government already had far less tax revenue relative to most countries which combined with its high debt load tax cuts would be dangerous. Samaraweera predicted that “If these proposals are implemented like this not only will the entire country go bankrupt, but the entire country will become another Venezuela or another Greece.”On 6 April 2022, the CBSL allegedly printed 119.08 billion rupees, making it the highest reported amount printed on a single day by the CBSL for the year 2022. The total money added to financial markets for the year 2022 increased to Rs. 432.76 billion.

External debt
Until mid-2000s, the Sri Lankan debt was mainly from multilateral lending agencies, after which it was reoriented under the leadership of Mahinda Rajapaksa to foreign investors and lenders. Sri Lanka issues its first international sovereign bond in 2007, with high interest rates to incentivise investors. According to commentators, the money was used to fund vanity projects rather than projects of national utility.Sri Lanka's foreign debt increased substantially, going from US$11.3 billion in 2005 to $56.3 billion in 2020. While foreign debt was about 42% of the GDP in 2019, it rose to 119% of its GDP in 2021. By February 2022, the country had only $2.31 billion left in its reserves, yet faces debt repayments of around $4 billion in 2022, which also includes a $1 billion international sovereign bond (ISB) maturing in July.In 2020, US economist Joseph Eugene Stiglitz, published a report that blamed the quantitative easing policy made by US banks after 2008, for exporting debt bubbles to deve

. This has raised concerns about the country's ability to meet its financial obligations and maintain its economic stability.

The declining reserves can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, the COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted the country's economy, leading to a decrease in export revenues and foreign direct investment. This has resulted in a decline in foreign currency inflows, putting pressure on the country's reserves.

Secondly, the country has been facing a persistent current account deficit, meaning that it is importing more goods and services than it is exporting. This has further strained the country's reserves as it needs to use foreign currency to pay for these imports.

Additionally, the country has been grappling with high levels of external debt. The debt repayments, including the maturing ISB, add to the financial burden and put further strain on the country's reserves.

To address these challenges, the country may need to take several measures. Firstly, it could seek financial assistance from international organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or the World Bank. This could provide the country with the necessary funds to meet its debt obligations and stabilize its reserves.

Secondly, the country could implement policies to boost its export revenues and reduce its reliance on imports. This could include promoting domestic industries, diversifying its export markets, and improving the business environment to attract foreign investment.

Furthermore, the country could explore options to restructure its debt, such as negotiating with creditors to extend repayment periods or reduce interest rates. This could help alleviate the immediate financial pressure and provide the country with more breathing room to manage its reserves.

Overall, the declining reserves and upcoming debt repayments pose significant challenges for the country's economic stability. However, with the right measures and support from international organizations, the country can work towards addressing these challenges and ensuring its long-term financial sustainability.

contexts:
The Sri Lankan economic crisis is an ongoing crisis in the island country of Sri Lanka that started in 2019. It is the country's worst economic crisis since its independence in 1948. It has led to unprecedented levels of inflation, near-depletion of foreign exchange reserves, shortages of medical supplies, and an increase in prices of basic commodities. The crisis is said to have begun due to multiple compounding factors like tax cuts, money creation, a nationwide policy to shift to organic or biological farming, the 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in Sri Lanka. The subsequent economic hardships resulted in the 2022 Sri Lankan protests.
Sri Lanka had been earmarked for sovereign default, as the remaining foreign exchange reserves of US$1.9 billion as of March 2022 would not be sufficient to pay the country's foreign debt obligations for 2022, with $4 billion to be repaid. An International Sovereign Bond repayment of $1 billion was due to be paid by the government in July 2022. Bloomberg reported that Sri Lanka had a total of $8.6 billion in repayments due in 2022, including both local debt and foreign debt. In April 2022, the Sri Lankan government announced that it was defaulting, making it the first sovereign default in Sri Lankan history since its independence in 1948 and the first state in the Asia-Pacific region to enter sovereign default in the 21st century.In June 2022, then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said in parliament that the economy had collapsed, leaving it unable to pay for essentials.In September 2022, a United Nations report said that the economic crisis is a result of officials' impunity for human rights abuses and economic crimes. According to the Sri Lankan finance ministry, the country's foreign reserves had grown by 23.5% from US$1.7 billion in September 2022 to US$2.1 billion in February 2023, representing a US$400 million increase. Sri Lanka teeters on the edge of financial insolvency and has halted repayments on its international debts.

Background
According to W. A. Wijewardena, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the country was a long way into an economic crisis in 2015. The government that came into power in 2015 knew this and had been warned by the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka about a number of risks. While the then Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe in 2015 had presented a strong economic policy to address the situation, the coalition government could not get the policy pushed through Parliament, which would eventually result in further policy confusion in the coming months.The government did not adequately address the economic warnings and emerging dangers, consuming itself in other government related activities such as "constitutional reforms". Certain practices, including those used by the Ministry of Finance led by Ravi Karunanayake, were globally frowned upon. Election related economic decisions were pushed such as excessive distribution of freebies. The Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka's 2014 State of the Economy Report highlighted hot money, worrying borrowing practices, temporary and superficial quick-fixes and monopoly of foreign direct investment flow into the hospitality sector.Further political turmoil in 2018 worsened the economic outlook. By that time the government had carried out several reforms under an IMF supported program towards fiscal monetary consolidation and had successfully controlled inflation. These reforms included an automatic fuel pricing formula which significantly reduced fiscal risks posed by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), raised the value-added tax (VAT) rate from 11 percent to 15 percent, and broadened the VAT base by removing exemptions. Many of the reforms were reversed by the new government after the 2019 elections.Under Maithripala Sirisena administration, the 2019 Central Bank Bill was drafted to make the Central Bank independent from political influence by banning the Treasury Secretary and any member of the Government from becoming members of the Monetary Board. Money printing was also to be banned under this bill, as it states: "The Central Bank shall not purchase securities issued by the government, by any government-owned entity, or any other public entity in the primary market." Then Central Bank Governor, Indrajit Coomaraswamy, noted Balance of Payments issues, increased inflation, and asset bubbles as reasons for the ban. The Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna Party opposed an independent Central Bank and discarded the bill as soon as they came to power.Many experts compared Lebanon's economic situation with that of Sri Lanka and had warned that Sri Lanka too was on the way to defaulting on its sovereign bonds. Both nations had similar issues, including deep economic crises occurring after their successive governments piled up unsustainable debts following the end of civil wars. To reduce the inflation and control the economy crisis in April 2022, Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe was appointed as the 17th Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) to replace Ajith Nivard Cabraal.

Causes
Tax cuts and money creation
The Government of Sri Lanka under president Gotabaya Rajapaksa made large tax cuts that affected government revenue and fiscal policies, causing budget deficits to soar.  These cuts included increased tax-free thresholds that resulted in a 33.5% decline in registered taxpayers, reducing VAT to 8%, reducing corporate tax from  28% to 24%, the abolishment of the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax and the 2% “nation-building tax” which financed infrastructure development. The massive loss of tax revenue resulted in rating agencies downgrading the sovereign credit rating making it harder to take more debt. In 2021 P. B. Jayasundera stated that President Rajapaksa was aware of the loss of revenue but considered it an "investment" and had no plans of increasing taxes for another 5 years.To cover government spending, the Central Bank began printing money in record amounts ignoring advice from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to stop printing money and instead hike interest rates and raise taxes while cutting spending.  The IMF warned that continuing to print money would lead to an economic implosion. The tax cuts were also opposed by the former Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera who noted that as the Sri Lankan government already had far less tax revenue relative to most countries which combined with its high debt load tax cuts would be dangerous. Samaraweera predicted that “If these proposals are implemented like this not only will the entire country go bankrupt, but the entire country will become another Venezuela or another Greece.”On 6 April 2022, the CBSL allegedly printed 119.08 billion rupees, making it the highest reported amount printed on a single day by the CBSL for the year 2022. The total money added to financial markets for the year 2022 increased to Rs. 432.76 billion.

External debt
Until mid-2000s, the Sri Lankan debt was mainly from multilateral lending agencies, after which it was reoriented under the leadership of Mahinda Rajapaksa to foreign investors and lenders. Sri Lanka issues its first international sovereign bond in 2007, with high interest rates to incentivise investors. According to commentators, the money was used to fund vanity projects rather than projects of national utility.Sri Lanka's foreign debt increased substantially, going from US$11.3 billion in 2005 to $56.3 billion in 2020. While foreign debt was about 42% of the GDP in 2019, it rose to 119% of its GDP in 2021. By February 2022, the country had only $2.31 billion left in its reserves, yet faces debt repayments of around $4 billion in 2022, which also includes a $1 billion international sovereign bond (ISB) maturing in July.In 2020, US economist Joseph Eugene Stiglitz, published a report that blamed the quantitative easing policy made by US banks after 2008, for exporting debt bubbles to deve

. This has raised concerns about the country's ability to meet its financial obligations and maintain its economic stability.

The declining reserves can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, the COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted the country's economy, leading to a decrease in export revenues and foreign direct investment. This has resulted in a decline in foreign currency inflows, putting pressure on the country's reserves.

Secondly, the country has been facing a persistent current account deficit, meaning that it is importing more goods and services than it is exporting. This has further strained the country's reserves as it needs to use foreign currency to pay for these imports.

Additionally, the country has been grappling with high levels of external debt. The debt repayments, including the maturing ISB, add to the financial burden and put further strain on the country's reserves.

To address these challenges, the country may need to take several measures. Firstly, it could seek financial assistance from international organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or the World Bank. This could provide the country with the necessary funds to meet its debt obligations and stabilize its reserves.

Secondly, the country could implement policies to boost its export revenues and reduce its reliance on imports. This could include promoting domestic industries, diversifying its export markets, and improving the business environment to attract foreign investment.

Furthermore, the country could explore options to restructure its debt, such as negotiating with creditors to extend repayment periods or reduce interest rates. This could help alleviate the immediate financial pressure and provide the country with more breathing room to manage its reserves.

Overall, the declining reserves and upcoming debt repayments pose significant challenges for the country's economic stability. However, with the right measures and support from international organizations, the country can work towards addressing these challenges and ensuring its long-term financial sustainability.

"Tapi, ibaratnya, mereka terlalu banyak menguras air dari sumur kita. Pendapatan pemerintah langsung anjlok drastis. Akibatnya, uang untuk membiayai kebutuhan negara menjadi sangat kurang."

Anya mengerutkan kening. "Jadi, seperti kalau ayahku gajinya dipotong, kita akan kesulitan membayar kebutuhan rumah tangga?"

"Tepat sekali, Anya! Karena pendapatan negara berkurang, lembaga pemeringkat internasional menurunkan peringkat kredit kita. Ini seperti bank yang menilai seseorang tidak mampu membayar utang, sehingga sulit bagi negara kita untuk meminjam uang lagi dari luar negeri."

**Faktor Kedua: Mencetak Uang Terlalu Banyak (Menggandakan Kertas, Bukan Kekayaan)**

"Karena uang pajak berkurang, pemerintah mencari cara lain untuk membiayai pengeluaran," lanjut Pak Wijaya. "Mereka mulai mencetak uang dalam jumlah besar. Ini seperti kalau kamu kekurangan uang jajan, lalu kamu menggambar uang sendiri di kertas. Apakah uang gambaran itu bisa membeli permen?"

Anya tertawa. "Tentu saja tidak, Paman!"

"Benar. Mencetak uang terlalu banyak tanpa didukung oleh produksi barang dan jasa yang nyata, justru membuat nilai uang kita jatuh. Ini namanya **inflasi**. Barang-barang menjadi sangat mahal karena uang yang beredar terlalu banyak, tapi barangnya tetap sama. Akibatnya, daya beli masyarakat menurun drastis. Ini yang membuat harga bensin, makanan, dan obat-obatan melambung tinggi."

**Faktor Ketiga: Pergeseran Pertanian Organik Mendadak (Menjatuhkan Sekop di Tengah Jalan)**

"Pernahkah kamu mendengar tentang kebijakan pertanian organik?" tanya Pak Wijaya. "Pemerintah kita saat itu memutuskan untuk melarang penggunaan pupuk kimia dan pestisida secara tiba-tiba, dengan harapan menjadi negara pertama di dunia yang sepenuhnya organik."

"Kedengarannya bagus, Paman. Lebih sehat, kan?" kata Anya.

"Memang tujuannya baik, Anya. Tapi pelaksanaannya terlalu mendadak dan tanpa persiapan yang matang. Petani kita belum siap dengan metode organik skala besar. Akibatnya, hasil panen, terutama beras dan teh (ekspor utama kita), anjlok drastis. Kita bahkan harus mengimpor beras, padahal dulu kita mandiri pangan."

"Ini seperti kamu sedang membangun rumah, lalu tiba-tiba semua tukang disuruh berhenti memakai alat modern dan hanya boleh memakai alat tradisional. Pekerjaan pasti jadi lambat dan hasilnya kurang maksimal," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Penurunan hasil pertanian ini berdampak besar pada ketersediaan pangan dan juga pemasukan devisa dari ekspor."

**Faktor Keempat: Serangan Teroris dan Pandemi (Badai Tak Terduga)**

"Selain masalah internal, ada juga badai dari luar," kata Pak Wijaya dengan nada prihatin. "Pada tahun 2019, terjadi serangan bom Paskah yang mengerikan. Ini sangat merusak industri pariwisata kita, yang merupakan salah satu sumber utama devisa negara."

"Lalu, pandemi COVID-19 datang. Pembatasan perjalanan dan penutupan perbatasan membuat pariwisata lumpuh total. Pekerja migran kita yang mengirimkan uang dari luar negeri juga banyak yang kehilangan pekerjaan. Akibatnya, pemasukan devisa negara semakin menipis."

Anya menghela napas. "Jadi, devisa itu seperti tabungan negara dalam mata uang asing, Paman?"

"Tepat sekali! Devisa sangat penting untuk membayar impor barang-barang penting seperti bahan bakar, obat-obatan, dan bahan baku industri. Ketika devisa menipis, kita tidak bisa membeli barang-barang ini dari luar negeri, sehingga terjadi kelangkaan dan harga semakin naik."

**Faktor Kelima: Utang Luar Negeri yang Menumpuk (Beban yang Terlalu Berat)**

"Sejak lama, Sri Lanka memiliki kebiasaan meminjam uang dari negara lain dan lembaga internasional," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Dulu, kebanyakan pinjaman untuk proyek pembangunan yang penting. "Utang ini terus menumpuk. Ketika devisa menipis, kita kesulitan membayar cicilan utang. Ini seperti kamu punya banyak utang kartu kredit, tapi gajimu dipotong dan kamu tidak bisa membayar cicilan. Akhirnya, kamu dinyatakan bangkrut."

"Ini adalah pelajaran berharga bahwa sebuah negara harus memiliki manajemen ekonomi yang hati-hati, perencanaan yang matang, dan tidak boleh mengambil keputusan penting secara terburu-buru tanpa mempertimbangkan dampaknya secara menyeluruh. Kita harus belajar dari kesalahan ini agar badai seperti ini tidak terulang lagi."

Anya mengangguk pelan, wajahnya menunjukkan pemahaman yang lebih dalam. "Terima kasih, Paman. Sekarang aku mengerti mengapa Sri Lanka kita mengalami kesulitan ini. Ini bukan hanya satu masalah, tapi banyak masalah yang terjadi bersamaan."

"Benar, Anya. Dan penting bagi kalian para generasi muda untuk memahami ini, agar kelak kalian bisa menjadi warga negara yang kritis dan berkontribusi dalam membangun masa depan yang lebih baik untuk Sri Lanka."

"Sejak lama, Sri Lanka memiliki kebiasaan meminjam uang dari negara lain dan lembaga internasional," jelas Pak Wijaya. "Dulu, kebanyakan pinjaman untuk proyek pembangunan yang penting. The Myanmar civil war (Burmese: ၂၀၂၁-၂၀၂၃ မြန်မာနိုင်ငံ ပြည်သူ့ခုခံတွန်းလှန်စစ်), also called the Myanmar Spring Revolution, and the People's Defensive War, is an ongoing civil war following Myanmar's long-running insurgencies which escalated significantly in response to the 2021 military coup d'état and the subsequent violent crackdown on anti-coup protests.In the months following the coup, the opposition began to coalesce around the National Unity Government, which launched an offensive against the junta. By 2022, the opposition controlled substantial, though sparsely populated, territory. In many villages and towns, the junta's attacks drove out tens of thousands of people. On the second anniversary of the coup, in February 2023, the chairman of the State Administration Council, Min Aung Hlaing, admitted to losing stable control over "more than a third" of townships. Independent observers note the real number is likely far higher, with as few as 72 out of 330 townships and all major population centres remaining under stable control.As of September 2022, 1.3 million people have been internally displaced, and over 13,000 children have been killed. By March 2023, the UN estimated that since the coup, 17.6 million people in Myanmar required humanitarian assistance, while 1.6 million were internally displaced, and 55,000 civilian buildings had been destroyed. UNOCHA said that over 40,000 people fled into neighboring countries.

Background
On the morning of 1 February 2021, the Myanmar military, or Tatmadaw, successfully deposed the elected Myanmar government in a coup, forming a military junta. Former president Win Myint, Aung San Suu Kyi, and several other members of the National League for Democracy were detained during early morning raids and Min Aung Hlaing was placed as the Commander-in-Chief of Defence Services and de facto ruler of the nation.The exact motives behind the coup are unclear. In the leadup to the coup, the Tatmadaw claimed that the 2020 general elections had 8.6 million voter irregularities, but presented no evidence. The coup may have been a way to re-establish the military's long-reigning power over the country which ended ten years prior.The bloody repression of anti-coup demonstrations led to the creation of armed groups to fight the State Administration Council, the military junta. Gathered under the name of the People's Defence Force (PDF) and the orders of the National Unity Government (NUG), formed by former parliamentarians in office before the coup d'état, the PDF and the NUG officially declared a "defensive war" against the military regime in September 2021. The ACLED estimated that as of 29 July 2022, around 23,521 people in total had been killed in the violence following the 2021 coup.

Existing conflict
Insurgencies have been ongoing in Myanmar since 1948 and have largely been ethnic-based. Communist insurgencies and the Karen National Union were the primary opposition actors to the central government. Over the 20th century, several prominent ethnic armed organisations (EAOs) rose and fell in influence and control. Larger rebel factions such as the Kachin Independence Army formed in response to Ne Win's 1962 Burmese coup d'état and its increased political repression. The 8888 Uprising in response to the totalitarian rule of Ne Win resulted in some of the first modern Bamar militias forming from protestors heading to areas under ethnic rebel control.
In the aftermath of the 8888 Uprising, the State Law and Order Restoration Council, later called the State Peace and Development Council, formed a military junta. The Tatmadaw severely weakened ethnic insurgent groups, destroying most of their bases and strongholds through the 1990s. By the time of the 2011–2015 Myanmar political reforms, the junta had regained control of many long-time rebel strongholds including Kokang and Karen State.As part of its political reforms and democratization, the 2008 Constitution created self-administered zones with increased autonomy. In 2015, the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) was signed between 8 EAOs and the central government. However, as soon as 2018, the NCA had already begun to fall apart due to alleged violations of the agreement by Tatmadaw soldiers entering EAO territories to build roads. Many non-signatories continued the conflict. In late 2016, four non-signatories of the NCA formed the Northern Alliance, including the Kachin Independence Army and Arakan Army, engaged in war with the central government and other EAOs.

Prelude
Armed protestors
In late March, dozens of protesters had travelled to Myanmar's border areas to enlist in and train under one of the country's many insurgent groups, elevating the risk of a countrywide civil war. The Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw also proposed the formation of a "federal armed force" to combat the military, and in late March the Arakan Army (AA) threatened to end its ceasefire with the military should the latter "persist in massacring civilians".During late March, protesters increasingly began arming themselves with homemade weapons such as guns in an attempt to defend themselves against attacks by the military. Simultaneously, clashes with soldiers and IED attacks against administrative buildings and police stations became more common as the trend of protesters using armed resistance rose.

Renewed ethnic conflict
The unrest across the nation and the increased need for junta troops in previously peaceful urban areas strengthened EAOs. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) has already been on the offensive against the military since February and seized the military base of Alaw Bum near the town of Laiza on 25 March. The next day, the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) attacked a military base, killing 10 soldiers and taking others hostages in the first attack on the military since the protests began. The following day saw the 2021 Kalay clashes, the first openly armed resistance by protesters in the town of Kalay against the junta. Protestors used homemade weapons against soldiers and security forces attacking a protest camp.The military junta declared that it would cease all military operations on 29 March and hold bilateral negotiations with ethnic armed groups. However, the KIA continued its offensives stating that the Myanmar Army had continued operations as usual. Through April, the informal clashes intensified, such as on 8 April when protesters fought back against soldiers with hunting rifles and firebombs in a battle that resulted in 11 protesters' deaths. The same day, the country surpassed 600 deaths related to anti-coup protests since 1 February.Seven insurgent groups who were signatories to the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement aligned themselves with the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw, including the All Burma Student Democratic Front and the Karen National Union. The Northern Alliance, comprising the Arakan Army, the Ta'ang National Liberation Army and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army, attacked a police station in Naungmon, Shan State, killing at least 10 police officers and indicating their disregard of the junta's call for a ceasefire. In response, on 11 April, the junta military launched a counter-attack to recapture the Alaw Bum base using airstrikes and ground troops, but had to retreat amidst heavy casualties.

New conflicts
On 26 April, the Battle of Mindat became one of the first large-scale conflicts arising from the 2021 coup. The Chinland Defense Force (CDF) began armed resistance in Mindat, Chin State. As a response, the junta cut off food and water supplies and declared martial law. Fighting began when a group of demonstrators outside the town's Aung San statue requested the release of six of their arrested colleagues, when a soldier of the regime allegedly fired at someone, prompting protesters to react.
According to an aid worker, more than 10,000 people have left Mindat in southern Chin State as the Myanmar military star

violently. The situation quickly escalated into a full-blown clash between the military and the protesters.

The military, armed with heavy weaponry and supported by armored vehicles, launched a brutal crackdown on the demonstrators. Tear gas, rubber bullets, and live ammunition were used indiscriminately, resulting in numerous casualties among the protesters. The streets of the town turned into a chaotic battleground, with fires burning and the sound of gunfire echoing through the air.

Despite the overwhelming force of the military, the protesters fought back with whatever they could find. They threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, and set up makeshift barricades to slow down the advancing troops. The clashes continued for hours, with both sides sustaining heavy losses.

As news of the violent clashes spread, more people from neighboring towns and villages joined the protest, swelling the ranks of the demonstrators. The military's attempts to quell the uprising only fueled the people's anger and determination to fight for their rights and freedom.

International condemnation poured in as reports of the brutal crackdown reached the global community. Calls for an immediate end to the violence and the release of all political prisoners grew louder. Diplomatic pressure was exerted on the junta, with sanctions and other punitive measures threatened if the violence did not cease.

Inside the town, the fighting raged on. The protesters, fueled by their desire for justice and democracy, refused to back down. They formed a network of underground resistance, organizing protests, strikes, and acts of civil disobedience to disrupt the military's control.

The junta, realizing the growing resistance and international pressure, eventually agreed to enter into negotiations with the protesters. A ceasefire was declared, and talks began to find a peaceful resolution to the crisis. However, the trust between the two sides was shattered, and the road to reconciliation would be long and arduous.

The town's Aung San statue, once a symbol of hope and unity, now stood as a reminder of the violence and bloodshed that had taken place. The scars of the conflict would take time to heal, but the people's determination to fight for their rights remained unbroken. They knew that the struggle for democracy was far from over, and they were willing to continue the fight, no matter the cost.

"Nah, itu poin penting, Aung," Guru Maya mengangguk. "Myanmar memang punya sejarah panjang konflik etnis yang sudah ada sejak kemerdekaan. Kelompok-kelompok etnis bersenjata (EAO) sudah lama berjuang untuk otonomi. Tapi, kudeta 2021 ini memperburuk situasi dan menciptakan konflik baru. Bahkan, beberapa kelompok etnis yang sudah memiliki perjanjian gencatan senjata dengan pemerintah sebelumnya, kini ikut bergabung melawan junta."

**Bab 4: Status Perang Saudara Saat Ini: Pertarungan yang Berlangsung**

"Jadi, bagaimana status perang saudara Myanmar saat ini?" Guru Maya menatap Aung dengan serius. "Ini adalah konflik yang kompleks dan terus berkembang."

"Dua tahun setelah kudeta, pada Februari 2023, pemimpin junta, Min Aung Hlaing, mengakui bahwa mereka telah kehilangan kendali stabil atas 'lebih dari sepertiga' kota praja. Tapi, pengamat independen percaya angka sebenarnya jauh lebih tinggi. Mereka memperkirakan hanya sekitar 72 dari 330 kota praja, dan beberapa pusat populasi besar, yang masih berada di bawah kendali stabil militer."

"Ini berarti, sebagian besar wilayah Myanmar, terutama di pedesaan, berada di bawah kendali atau setidaknya pengaruh kelompok-kelompok perlawanan dan EAO. Pertempuran masih terus terjadi di banyak tempat, dan militer sering menggunakan kekuatan udara untuk menyerang wilayah yang dikuasai perlawanan."

"Tidak, Aung. Mereka menghadapi perlawanan yang kuat dari berbagai penjuru. Perang ini telah mengubah banyak desa dan kota menjadi medan pertempuran, memaksa puluhan ribu orang untuk meninggalkan rumah mereka."

**Bab 5: Angka-Angka yang Memilukan: Pengungsian Internal**

"Dan inilah bagian yang paling menyedihkan, Aung," Guru Maya melanjutkan, suaranya melembut. "Konflik ini telah menyebabkan krisis kemanusiaan yang sangat besar."

"Pertanyaanmu tadi adalah: berapa banyak orang yang mengungsi secara internal sejak kudeta? Angka itu terus meningkat. Pada September 2022, PBB memperkirakan sudah ada **1,3 juta orang** yang mengungsi secara internal. Ini berarti mereka terpaksa meninggalkan rumah mereka tetapi masih berada di dalam wilayah Myanmar."

"Dan pada Maret 2023, PBB melaporkan bahwa jumlah pengungsi internal telah meningkat menjadi **1,6 juta orang**. Bayangkan, 1,6 juta orang kehilangan tempat tinggal, harus hidup dalam ketidakpastian, seringkali tanpa akses yang memadai ke makanan, air bersih, atau layanan kesehatan."

Aung terdiam, membayangkan jutaan orang yang kehilangan segalanya. "Itu jumlah yang sangat besar, Bu. Dan anak-anak?"

"Sayangnya, anak-anak adalah korban paling rentan," Guru Maya menghela napas. "Hingga September 2022, lebih dari **13.000 anak-anak** telah terbunuh dalam kekerasan ini. Selain itu, PBB memperkirakan bahwa 17,6 juta orang di Myanmar membutuhkan bantuan kemanusiaan, dan 55.000 bangunan sipil telah hancur. Bahkan, lebih dari 40.000 orang telah melarikan diri ke negara-negara tetangga."

**Bab 6: Harapan di Tengah Kegelapan**

"Jadi, perang ini masih terus berlangsung, Bu?"

"Ya, Aung. Perang saudara Myanmar ini adalah konflik yang berkelanjutan. Meskipun situasinya sangat menantang, semangat perlawanan rakyat Myanmar tidak padam. Mereka terus berjuang untuk demokrasi dan hak-hak asasi mereka."

Aung mengangguk perlahan, wajahnya menunjukkan campuran kesedihan dan pemahaman. "Terima kasih, Bu Maya. Saya sekarang lebih mengerti. Ini jauh lebih kompleks dari yang saya bayangkan."

"Itulah tujuan belajar sejarah dan kewarganegaraan, Aung. Untuk membuka mata kita terhadap realitas dunia, dan mungkin, suatu hari nanti, untuk menjadi bagian dari solusi," Guru Maya tersenyum, mengakhiri pelajaran hari itu.
